utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have one or two matters to deal with before we continue with the evidence. Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm to bring to your attention the fact that translations of two of your expert reports has not yet been provided by the time that you indicated they would be provided. That's Mr. Stamenov, the 16th of July, and Mr. Garovic, the 18th of July. Do you have any comments on that? Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Our assistant just told us that we had received the document yesterday. We had a lot of work, but -- and I'm very sorry for being late, but we are preparing a new motion, and we will disclose all the translation of the reports by tomorrow. I really apologise to my -- to the parties, but we received them yesterday, and we didn't have enough time to prepare the notification, but we will do it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes, because the evidence of those witnesses will be taken in the one week in which we are sitting in August. May we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you have any matter to raise, Mr. Waespi, or is it Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be very brief. Thank you for allowing me to address you quite briefly. Yesterday, we received 54 documents of the United Nations in accordance with Rule 66 and 68. These were the documents in relation to which a waiver was obtained within the spirit of Rule 70. This is the material we received yesterday. We are now in a situation where we do not know how to proceed with a view to using the material for our benefit, because this is not subject to disclosure. The material we simply scanned. We didn't have time to go through them thoroughly. And these are the United Nations documents in respect of which a waiver was obtained, which can therefore be used. I seek your guidance. We have to find a way to have these documents admitted into evidence. We are nearing the end of the case, and I simply do not know who to introduce the documents through. Perhaps through Mr. Demurenko. Possibly he may not know anything about them. This is, at any rate, a very delicate issue of crucial importance for the case. These were the documents to which we were barred access before, and we received them yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. These documents are not related to Mr. Demurenko. They are the fruits of a search we made a couple of months ago into what we believe these Rule 66(B) and perhaps 68 from the Defence perspective in relation to what's commonly known as suffering, the presence of Bosnian irregulars like Caco and other people, which we understand is the Defence case. And we don't believe they are relevant for this case, but we understand that it's important for the Defence to have them. If the Defence feels that documents are relevant for their case, these are genuine UN, usually UNPROFOR, documents which speak for themselves, we certainly have no objections if they're relevant to them coming in as self-propelled documents without any tendering witness. We certainly have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wasn't in fact aiming at anything else but this, and I wish to thank my learned friend Mr. Waespi. I was of the same opinion. When we looked at the documents, we realised that they were very significant for the Defence and are self-evident. We deemed it very important that the Chamber grant leave for their admission into evidence, which we hope that the Chamber will do having heard our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll give you a decision later today. Let the witness be brought in. Mr. Tapuskovic, of course we would want to see the documents. How do we see them? Are they in the electronic system?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. On a CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which is different. We disclosed them on a CD to the Defence anticipating that if they want to use one or two, because clearly in our view they are not relevant, but who am I to tell what's relevant for the Defence. So if the Defence feels some are relevant, perhaps 54 of them, they obviously have the obligation to put it into the e-court system, and then they can be -- but Mr. President, we are happy to send you the CD or even hard copies of these 54 documents so you can peruse them and for your decision to admit them or not. We certainly would have an opinion on the relevancy of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They must be relevant -- they must be relevant to the case, not relevant to the Defence case or relevant to the Prosecution case. They must be relevant to the case. I don't know of the concept of relevance to a particular party's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we'll proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just on this, Mr. President. Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll have the CD copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We will forward it to you. Of course this is disclosure, and disclosure under Rule 66(B) means whatever is -- I think the term is material for the Defence, and by now we know pretty much what's material for the Defence. So that's our standard for disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand. Now, Mr. Sachdeva -- Mr. Sachdeva, you see this? It comes from the court deputy. It reminds me that you have used 1 hour and 17 minutes of 1 hour and 25 minutes allotted. You have one hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness T-41. I trust you rested well last night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when we closed -- or before we closed, I was showing you a video clip of -- of some positions on the Pale-Lukavica Road. You remember that clip, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I'm just going to ask for that clip -- I'm just going to ask for that clip to be brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness answered this question twice. What I wish to highlight is the very question put by Mr. Sachdeva. The positions on the Pale, et cetera, road, not once did the witness state that he had seen positions on the road, and the question as such was put already twice. I am referring to the transcript. Since my learned friend Sachdeva has now repeated once again these were positions on the road, can he please indicate on the photograph where does it show that the positions were on the road -- or, rather, I meant on this video clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm waiting to hear the question. The question hasn't been put yet. What is the question you wish to put, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I need to wait for the clip to be shown, but if I might just briefly respond to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to -- you have on your screen there, you have a picture of a rifle. You see that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see a weapon of a sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, sir, that the -- the contraption that is fitted on top of the rifle is, I would suggest to you, a contraption that facilitates -- facilitates enhanced viewing. In other words, it is an optical sight. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I never looked through any such item. I can see that this is a rifle, but I never had this device in my hands to be 100 per cent sure of what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I appreciate that you may not be 100 per cent sure, but I'm just suggesting to you, sir, that that contraption that is on top of the rifle is most probably an optical sight to facilitate an enhanced view. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't accept that before I see what it looks like in reality or on a much better image.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't see the rifle grenades that were, as you said, fired by the ABiH, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw parts of the projectile. Sometime when there was fire going on I saw parts of the grenades that did not explode. I think I saw a Maljutka that -- at least it was explained to me that this is what it was. It had some wiring on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking you about what came from the weapon or the projectiles, but you never saw the rifle grenade weapon that you said was fired by the ABiH. You never saw that weapon allegedly fired by the ABiH, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that, nor could I. I only saw the consequences of it. I saw a shell falling, and it could only have come from the ABH positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution moves to tender this -- this clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P910, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday in answers to questions by Counsel Tapuskovic you said that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps press centre was established in December 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that you were working at this centre throughout the conflict up until November 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked at the press centre in the period mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that the -- the office or the room that -- where the press centre was located was in the same building at Lukavica where, firstly, General Galic and thereafter General Milosevic had their offices; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, the press centre was on the ground floor right next to the entrance. The journalists went there. I didn't move much. I only went to the kitchen there. Later on the press centre was relocated to a different part of the building -- or, rather, these are two buildings that are very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When the press centre was in the ground floor and then when it moved, it was in the same building as the office of General Milosevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't in the same building, but it was very close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, yesterday you told Mr. Tapuskovic, you told the Court that when the press centre was in the ground floor of the building that on the next floor, the next floor above the ground floor was where General Milosevic had his office, or General Galic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I believe it was upstairs. Upstairs there were offices where General Milosevic was, and his escorts would sometimes come over to my office and talk to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps press centre how many -- how many people or how many soldiers worked at the centre? And I'm interested in -- well, throughout the conflict but specifically in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning when the press centre was formed, there were three or four of us there. Journalists would come and go. Later on the press centre got more personnel. The journalists were doing their job preparing what had to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so in the period 1994/1995, did you have -- did you have a supervisor, as it were, or was there somebody that you reported to within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps press centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were immediately subordinated to the assistant corps commander. When they needed us to do something, he would come over to let us know, or he would call us over the phone and tell us that we had to go somewhere or that journalists had to prepare a news report and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the assistant corps commander, as I understand it, in 1994 and 1995, was that Cedo Sladoje? Is that who you're speaking about? And if it's not, please tell the Court the name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that person. He was not in charge of the press centre. Another person was in charge of the press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was a colonel, but he was someone who wasn't from the area. He had come from elsewhere, and I simply can't recall his name. If you can give me a name, I'd perhaps be able to confirm it. Dragicevic. Actually, I believe his surname was Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it perhaps Luka, Luka Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. His name was Luka Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at the time in 1994, 1995, Luka Dragicevic was -- was the commander for the -- the unit -- the units -- commander of the morale, political and religious affairs unit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. He was in touch with the press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it that you -- in that period 1994/1995, you personally had regular dealings with Colonel Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we simply didn't have any regular dealings. If he needed something, he would come to the press centre or he would call over the phone and tell us that a crew would come and that somebody should take the crew out into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, can we agree, sir, that you at least had dealings with him, whether by telephone or in person, you or any of your colleagues, at least once a week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly we had to have contact. There was always something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you or any of your colleagues participate in the -- the regular corps command meetings? In other words, when General Milosevic held his meetings at the corps command, did you ever participate or any of your colleagues ever participate in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't participate in the meetings. Only sometimes when meetings were organised and we were invited to the meetings, but the command wasn't there. Perhaps it would just be a meeting at the press centre, talks, planning, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, do you remember having a meeting with General Milosevic, having an official meeting, not just you and him, but you and other members of the corps command, at all during the period 1994/1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about that, but I think that there were some meetings. It was a long time ago. I can't really say now with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in the -- in the press -- the press office or the press centre, what sort of equipment or facilities did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were just some desks, cupboards. There was a bed. I had my own camera. I obtained a camera that I used to make photographs, and somebody brought a video camera, a VHS camera. I don't know who it belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yesterday you told the Court that after you would take foreign journalists around the Serb part of Sarajevo and around the front lines, you would then monitor the press thereafter and see whether your -- your visits or your reports were featured in subsequent press reports. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked with a lot of TV crews. The press conferences were not ever held at the corps press centre. Only on one occasion when there was something about the pulling out of the artillery. And I tried to follow the media as much as I could. We had one or two programmes when we had electricity. The picture was pretty bad, the TV screen picture, and we tried to follow. I was simply interested to see how this was reported, how the journalists that I worked with that day would report on the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so I take it then you had -- you had a TV. You had a TV in your office in the press centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had an old TV that stayed there from the JNA. It broke down quite frequently. We didn't have a good antenna, so we improvised just to be able to follow something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you were able to follow, as you said, something on occasion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to follow. The signals were very weak in any case, and simply we just got more annoyed sometimes, and sometimes we were able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you were able to follow -- well, let me ask you this -- the foreign journalists that you took around during the conflict, yesterday you spoke about a team of British or English journalists that had come from Belgrade. Do you remember which companies or which countries the foreign journalists that you took around came from during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday's case when we watched the footage, I know that I got into a car and I was told there was a TV crew coming that was being guided by another person, and I used the opportunity to get to Grbavica with them. Many TV crews came. I know CNN would come, also some French channels. I know that there were also Italian TV crews, German ones. I remember their logos, and so that's how I could tell that these were TV crews. A lot of people circulated, but I wasn't the only one who escorted them, there were others also that worked on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you mentioned CNN, you mentioned French and German, and perhaps isn't it not -- is it not right, sir, that perhaps the BBC also came? The British Broadcasting Corporation from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would see those crews, but I didn't speak with them particularly. Perhaps I wasn't the one to escort them. I know that there were many, many crews from conversations, and I did see that there were people from the BBC also.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago that if needed Mr. Dragicevic would contact you or contact the press centre. What sort of things would he be asking of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already answered in a way. It would be to say that someone who was free or somebody would be assigned to take the TV crew where the TV crew -- team wanted to go or where they were permitted to go, where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When -- when you had undertaken these -- these excursions with these foreign journalists, and as you said you -- you sometimes were able to monitor the press subsequently to see how the reports had transpired, did you relay -- at times did you relay the information? In other words, did you speak to members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps about how these reports transpired, whether they -- they reported correctly or accurately? Did you do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I talked with the soldiers, and there was distrust on the part of the Serb soldiers towards the media, probably because of earlier reports or because of something. I don't know. It's not up to me to analyse. But I can answer your question by saying that I did talk. I don't know who I talked with. It's something that happened 12 or 13 years back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, for example, if the -- the French correspondents or perhaps the British correspondents from the BBC after accompanying the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps press centre on their trips then produced -- subsequently produced a report which you deemed -- after watching it which you deemed to be not completely accurate, that information, I take it, would be communicated to -- to Mr. Dragicevic or other members of the Sarajevo Corps command. Is that how I understand it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was supposed to inform some of the persons in charge, I would have done that. We simply didn't pay attention to that. And there was constant distrust in some way towards these foreign electronic media on the part of the soldiers. So that's the only thing I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I appreciate the distrust that you say there was, but during your time at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps press centre, in other words, during the period of the conflict you did, did you not, you did recount the contents of these media reports that you monitored. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Rarely. It's possible, but I don't recall anyone asking me to go and say I was with these people, or if I met somebody I could say I was there, I completed the assignment, everything is all right. Things like that. As I said, there were other people, other staff in the press centre, military conscripts, so I really cannot directly say that I recall anything. Possibly there were such things, but specifically, at this moment I cannot recall anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate you say it's possible that you might have done, but it's also possible that your other colleagues at the press centre did so as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. I couldn't do it myself. Sometimes you would have two, three, four crews turn up at the same time, so somebody would have to take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago about the distrust of the foreign media, and I take it that when you speak about that you are referring to the -- the stories from CNN, from the BBC, of how the civilians in Sarajevo were -- were under shell-fire and sniper-fire. Are those the sorts of stories that you're speaking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way it is connected, but this distrust, I personally also had that with the electronic media. I took two crews with me and I was going to show them Serb victims, people who had suffered on the Serb side. Simply they were not interesting in filming that; they wanted some other things like that. And I was even insulted then, and I saw that some of those crews are coming -- or were coming with a specific intention, and they reported more from Sarajevo, and it was as if they were doing it just because they were assigned to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So the -- you yourself and your colleagues and I would imagine other soldiers at Lukavica, when they -- when they got wind or when they on occasion managed to -- to monitor the foreign media, the BBC, the CNN, the French, and the reports contained images of civilians suffering within -- within the confrontation lines in Sarajevo, images of civilians being shelled or sniped, generally at Lukavica there was -- there was this distrust about those reports. Is that a fair statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way you could say that, but every time the crews came we didn't pay attention if they reported about something. Simply the person who was guiding the crew would become friendly with them. We didn't put any limits on their work. But definitely there was a kind of distrust. How can I put it? Simply, it was as if they were more leaning towards the Bosniak side, something like that. And we didn't really follow the reports or anything, but this is what I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when we talk about the suffering on the Bosniak side, I take it we mean within the confrontation lines of Sarajevo. So we're speaking about -- I would imagine we're speaking about incidents such as the Markale incident, such as the -- the incident -- the shelling of the waterline incident in Dobrinja, those sorts of incidents. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly these were events. I don't know which TV crews were covering that. In any case, it was the television of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the television that was under Bosniak control. They broadcast some news and we watched that. I don't know exactly if I can answer you the way you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to answer in a way that I want. I just want the truth from you, sir. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I have one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, may I just ask one question. Do you know or did you know when you worked in Lukavica of -- of somebody called Milenko Indjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say you knew him, did you meet with him? Did you have occasion to meet with him or be in meetings where he was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a liaison officer, liaison with the United Nations, and if anything was related to the press centre or any event that had to do with the United Nations, he would inform us. We would simply receive information from him. I mean, these were the contacts that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, for example, what kind of information did you receive from him? If you can remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know in 1995 that he was in a meeting in town where they discussed a shell that was fired at the airport and that they confirmed that this was fired from the Muslim, from the Bosniak side. And this report was sent to Zagreb, and he conveyed this information to the media that were in Lukavica. And if some meeting was supposed to take place, some politicians to meet, he would inform the press centre or one of the journalists to let them know that the journalists should wait, that these politicians, these persons were supposed to meet. They would provide transportation for those people. And they also were servicing the United Nations. And sometimes when these people were expected, the journalists would be waiting in these places where the meeting would take place. And when the meeting was over then Indjic would come and inform the journalists that they could go and speak to whoever was there at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did Colonel Indjic ever relate to you or your fellow colleagues, or did you ever hear about the -- the protests from the United Nations since he was the liaison officer, as you said, that protests he would have received from the United Nations about the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps shelling and sniping civilians in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, not personally to me, but if there were some -- if there were some cases like that I'm sure that he would convey that to people who were more authorised or were supposed to be dealing with matters like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I guess you mean -- you mean persons like Mr. Sladoje or Mr. -- in fact, General Milosevic. That's who you're speaking about, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think you understood me here. You asked the question whether the colonel or the major Indjic, whichever he was, conveyed that to us at the press centre. He did not do that. He did not convey that to me because I was not a journalist. But I don't know to whom he conveyed this information. I wasn't even supposed to know things like that. I'm just telling you about the type of work that I carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you agree that he probably would have conveyed this information to persons who were more authorised or who were supposed to be dealing with those matters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know what he conveyed, what the meetings were, what the system was, the system of command, because I simply wasn't in a position to know whether any sort of meeting of the command was held or not. I was simply not aware, or I wasn't informed about things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you were in the command, weren't you, as you said yesterday? You were in the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In other words, your unit was attached to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We were a separate section, and the press centre was formed quite late, and simply the journalists or anyone from the press centre did not go to any meetings so that we would know. Only when something needed to be done, then they would inform us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, isn't it right, sir, that in May, sometime thereabouts in May 1994, General Galic established what was known as a committee to produce the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps monograph? Is that something you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that this was discussed and that I was supposed to go and tour the entire corps region and to photograph that, but at that point it was not possible. I simply didn't have enough equipment. It wasn't possible to get enough film. So I just went and I made some photographs, and I waited for the material to arrive to be able to continue to work on this publication. I was very interested in making these photographs. I was making -- taking the photographs, but I didn't have the paper in order to be able to print them. All I had was the film, not the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And this -- this monograph, it was some sort of war record of the activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from 1992 to 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the idea. But it's something that was very hard to get going. My task was to take the photographs, take photographs of the Serbian soldiers in certain places, to photograph handsome, neat soldiers, to go around this whole area. However, this didn't come to anything practically because at the time I didn't have enough material. There were also some other factors that prevented that. I don't know who was in charge of perhaps writing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The -- wasn't the chairman of this committee Major General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and this is the first time that I'm hearing that a commission was formed and that General Milosevic would be at the head of that commission. In any case, I was entrusted with taking or making the photographs. However, we didn't have material. It was not possible for us to actually print the photograph. We were waiting for the material to arrive for the photographs to be printed and then to make this brochure or this publication, but we really couldn't complete the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask that the information you've just given has already been given to us, so please just try to stick to the questions I'm asking. Now, isn't it also correct that the deputy chairman was Colonel Ljubo Kosovac? Is that something that you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Ljubo Kosovac was before Colonel Dragicevic. He was at that post. And I know that Ljubo Kosovac -- I think it was Ljubo. Kosovac in any case is his last name. He told me I should be working on this publication and that I should be preparing material, photographs to go and make the photographs when the necessary material became available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document, and perhaps it might -- it might jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for 65 ter 03450 to be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you see on the right-hand side of the screen --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask for this not to be broadcast. Can I confirm that it's not being broadcast? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, sir you see at the top it's dated 17th of May, 1994, and that it comes from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the date again? I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's at the top. 17th of May, 1994. Top -- the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are numbers here that I cannot understand. I'm not sure that this first part of the number is a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, we can agree that it's 1994, can't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you look under item -- if you look under item 2, it states that: "An editorial board of the following members shall be responsible for producing the monograph," and the first name you see there is the chairman, "predsednik," Major General Dragomir Milosevic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we could move to the third page in the English. And you'll see, sir, that item 8 that it states that: "The commands of the units shall include in this material items on the engagement of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party; the Crisis Staff, the Orthodox Church, the Ministry of the Interior and the municipalities ..." You see that written there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do and I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see that it's signed by General Galic at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P911 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, just for -- to be sure that I have not overlooked something, what is it you wish exactly to show the Court by admitting this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I understand. The relevance -- I submit that the relevance is this: The -- the document clearly shows that in 1994, in May, when the accused was, as is recorded here, already a general and the chief of staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that he was responsible for the production of a record of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps combat activities, I suggest, and the activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And therefore, in our submission it goes to -- notice to the accused as we have alleged in our indictment that when Dragomir Milosevic was -- when the accused was the chief of staff prior to taking over the command, he would have -- we suggest would have been -- would have knowledge of the activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, would have knowledge of the crimes -- alleged crimes of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and taken that knowledge with him as he became commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So in our submission this -- this is part of that circumstantial evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I will not be raising any matters. If the document is admitted as a Prosecution exhibit, I will deal with it in my re-examination. I only wish to state the following: When you will be assessing the relevance of the document, you have to keep in mind the fact that the witness said that he had known about that and that this was a project that had never been materialised. I merely wanted the Trial Chamber to keep this in mind whilst deciding its weight, and of course I will deal with this matter in my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness did speak to having taken photographs and going -- in his role at least, going to -- to areas where Serbian soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not that. Continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I apologise. Is -- can I ask if the document is admitted under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admitted it. Under seal, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you said when I asked you questions about this document, you said that you did manage to go around the Serbian -- the Serb part of Sarajevo and take photographs of Serbian soldiers in certain locations. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you remember where these locations were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that in essence. However, when I started working on the monograph, I never saw this document. I went to a factory in the Vojkovic neighbourhood, and I spent an entire film there because I took photographs for the purposes of the monograph. I photographed the factory which had been damaged, devastated. It was divided between the two sides, the Bosniak and the Serb sides. I went to the Vojkovic neighbourhood also to take photographs of some soldiers and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that Mr. Sachdeva has used up the time given to him for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And so indeed you have, Mr. Sachdeva. You can have another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about your role with your camera, and we spoke yesterday about the -- about the photographs you took of the effects -- the effects of war in the Sarajevo -- the Serbian Sarajevo part. Did you ever photograph SRK troops in action? In other words, did you ever photograph Sarajevo-Romanija troops -- Sarajevo-Romanija Corps troops engaged in operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never at the front lines. I was always in the rear where you could hear gunfire and fighting, but I never went or joined the soldiers at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you still maintain your evidence that when you were at -- well, when you were going about with your camera along the -- in the Sarajevan -- Serb Sarajevan part of Sarajevo, you never wore a uniform or rarely; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wore a uniform rarely; only on occasions. It depended. Only if someone was coming. I also wore my uniform sometimes because I had a shortage of clothes. Especially in the wintertime when I wore a uniform jacket and I tried to make do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you wore your uniform by coincidence, did you have a rank, a military rank which was showing on that uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had never had a rank, and I had never worn uniforms with such insignia. It only could have happened that I borrowed someone's clothes. I know that in winter I didn't have enough winter clothes and I would on occasion borrow pieces of clothing from people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must be at an end now, Mr. Sachdeva. Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. When speaking of the problems concerning clothing, he said that he had these problems because he was a refugee and this was not reflected in the transcript, that he was a refugee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful to you for that, Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Sachdeva, you must close now. The very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were never at the front lines and you were in the rear, but -- but it is correct as you said to the Court yesterday, that you would go to these areas that were under constant threat and take photographs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was quite close to these positions. Yesterday, on one of the photographs you saw that I was passing behind soldiers in an actual war zone where danger is quite serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. This time I will have a number of questions. Since document P911 is still on our screens, let us first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. It's on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the screen, and that's why I wish to use it now rather than go back to it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read what is contained under item 10. You said something about that in answer to Mr. Sachdeva's question, but look at paragraph 10 and read that bit out, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean I should read it out aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just two lines of it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The monograph will be printed by the printing press in Ilidza. The means for its printing and the computer for text preparation for printing shall be provided by the Ilidza municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago in answer to the Prosecutor's question, you said this never materialised. I'm asking you now the following: The resources, the funds that are mentioned here, were they at all procured? Were they collected? Was it at all possible under war circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard the matter mentioned at the press centre, but nothing ever came out of that. We were never called by the Ilidza printing press to discuss this matter, and this is the first time I see this, in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we are still on this page, does any of the paragraphs here, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, mention any crimes? Mr. Sachdeva was stating something quite different to that. Are there any crimes mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't see anything of the sort. The concept of the monograph was not discussed to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I, just for the record, did not state that this document had those words or that content in this document. I was answering a question from His Honour Judge Harhoff as to the relevance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let us look at page 1, please. I have to dwell on this document for some time. Page 1. Above the line where it says "Order," can you read that passage and then I will have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Based on an apparent need and with the aim of professionally dealing with the historic material in the SRK monograph."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall this being mentioned in the discussions you had, that is to say the historic material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that something had to be done about that, and I knew that I personally could not deal with any historic material. This had to be done by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the names that are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in private session, by the way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think so. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, we're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session just for a moment? I have to read out a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any questions in relation to this because you know that yesterday the photographs, D326 MFI and 325 MFI, were in fact admitted only as MFI documents because of the poor quality. In order to save time, I would like to show both of these photographs on the ELMO, and after that they could be given their proper exhibit number. Your Honours, I have them in e-court as well. DD004288. Your Honours, in order not to waste any more time - something must be wrong with e-court - let's place this on the ELMO. There, Your Honours, the photograph is quite clear now, and could it be assigned a Defence exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I said yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could have the document ID number stated again or the MFI number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 325 MFI.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will remain Exhibit 325, D325.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if the same could be done with this other photograph which was yesterday assigned the following number: 326 MFI. And can we place it on the ELMO. The photograph in e-court is 325, whereas this photograph here is 326. Since the photograph we had yesterday was of very poor quality, we have a good copy now. Can it be assigned an exhibit number? Yesterday it was 326 MFI, and now it should be Defence Exhibit 326.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as D326.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have several questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two times you mentioned the name of Cedo Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you say you have several questions left. How long? Because it's time for the break. If it's just a minute or two, then we will take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will need 20 minutes certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to try to be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned in the cross-examination Luka Dragicevic, and you also mentioned Cedo Sladoje twice. At one point in time, was Cedo Sladoje practically carrying out the duties of commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how that works, but I know that he was one of the people who were in the corps. I don't know if he was a deputy. I don't know what the function was. I just know that he did functions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said at that Mr. Dragomir Milosevic went on sick leave in August 1995. Do you know who was performing the duties of the commander of the SRK at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think it was Colonel Sladoje. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that has to do with the document, the medical documentation, and yesterday you said that at the end of the examination of the witness you would put questions about the medical documents indicating something about the sick leave of Mr. Dragomir Milosevic in August, because this witness said that he knows that he was on sick leave at the time, and now he has just said what he has just said about Cedo Sladoje. Well, let me continue and finish, and then perhaps you will want to put those questions. I would like for us first to look at document of the Prosecution that we looked at yesterday. This is document P909.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You saw this photograph yesterday, is that correct, and you identified this as the home for the blind. Several questions about this were put to you by my learned friend Mr. Sachdeva, and you said that at the time you were passing. Do you know what caused these effects on this building from the time you saw it during the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I didn't see exactly. I don't know exactly what building this is, but evidently you can see here that this building burned. I don't know what happened to it. I can see that probably it was damaged or devastated in combat, in war activities. You can see it's damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Also yesterday, in response to specific questions by my learned friend Mr. Sachdeva, you explained these black traces on the side. Do you know what causes such markings on buildings when you see a marking like this, a trace like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you can still see these traces on some buildings in Sarajevo. These would be traces of an explosion or a smaller shell. I don't know what sort of calibre that could be. I think that these holes can be made only by some projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the film footage? This is document of the Prosecution, P910.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we stop it here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday there was a question about this -- well, do you see at all on this photograph anywhere a road, any kind of road anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any roads on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We were talking about Trebevic here. Can you say what the hills or elevations go to make up Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you go, then you can start from Vrace, Debelo Brdo, the observatory. I think those are the areas that connect to one another then there's the Prvi Sumar, Vidikovac. That's the place where the cable car used to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whose hill is the hill by the name Colina Kapa? Who held Colina Kapa? Under whose control was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two hills there that we in a way, I don't know exactly how, but I think this one part was held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I simply wasn't really passing by there so to know exactly and to be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, Witness, can you say under whose control this place was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell here. This photograph is technically bad, and simply there are no parameters that would allow me to recognise anything on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you also answer the question since my colleague Mr. Sachdeva asked you, rifle and then what was on it. And is this, please -- is this, please, a rifle that you see on this photograph here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You can see something. Perhaps it's a weapon. I mean it's dark. I don't know how close the person who took the photograph was so I cannot really tell exactly what it is. This is something bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And do you see the ammunition belt? Let's not waste time and show it from a different angle, but do you see the ammunition belt here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is some sort of ammunition that is going into the barrel. That's what it looks like to me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you at least tell me is this a rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is a rifle. I think this is a machine-gun. I don't know. The machine-guns would use the ammunition belts like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And now if we can just -- no, actually, I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. I take it you are finished, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I have, but you said yesterday -- you said that you would at the end of this examination deal with the medical document that indicates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D340, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can just do an additional thing. Yesterday I didn't have the original documents. I have the originals. I have copies, and I have the original documents which I can present to the Trial Chamber. These are original medical documents issued by the doctors at the clinic where he was treated. These are not copies. I have the original documents, and if it's necessary I can present the original documents of these documents that you have already admitted as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you can present them. If you have the originals, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the most important one. It has its contents on the first and the second page. It has its stamp, the signature of the doctor. I also have the accompanying documentation, but it seems to me that this is the most important document. It's been translated. It's a complete document. And this is the fifth and the sixth page in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just clarify through the Court whether these documents are the same documents or the same documents that were shown to the witness, because Mr. Tapuskovic is tendering this document through the witness, and therefore on account of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic informed me this was the original of the document which we admitted. That's the basis on which I've allowed him to -- to tender it. Is that so, Mr. Tapuskovic? If it's the original of the document that we have already admitted, then there is no problem. That suggests that the document admitted was a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can show -- I can show the documents to the Prosecution. This is a series of documents. They're all originals. The Prosecutor can look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The reason why -- the reason why I asked the question is because from my recollection the document that was shown to the witness was not five or six pages, and my recollection was that there was not handwritten information. I stand to be corrected, but that's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can look at the entire complete document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We are not dealing with the entire complete document. You asked me to allow you to tender the original of the document which we admitted. That was a very short document. What are you now seeking to do, to tender a number of other documents related to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. What already has been admitted, that is there, and that has been admitted. What I wanted to do is I wanted to strengthen that and say that I also have original documents. There is nothing new to what I had already tendered. This is DD003189, and I'm just saying I have the original documents, and I can also present them to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The document we admitted yesterday -- that we admitted today is an eight-page document. So the documents which you are presenting now, Mr. Tapuskovic are the originals of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, do you have anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I understand it, the page that was presented -- the document that was presented to the witness yesterday was -- was one page, as it seems to be in e-court. I don't recall -- perhaps it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear from the court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't recall exactly how many pages were shown to the witness. However, it's been standard practice in the proceeding to have multiple pages in one document and not show every single page to the witness in order to have that one document tendered and admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And how many pages were the document from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document that is currently in e-court. The document ID number is DD003189, is an eight-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I remember these documents. The medical history of Mr. Milosevic were shown to the first Defence witness, Mr. Veljovic, and I think at that time we didn't have translations. I think it's wrong to tender these documents through this witness, because the only thing can -- he can say is yes, I remember he was in Belgrade. But we do not object to have these documents come in as such because they say what they say. But to tender it with this witness, I think the link is just not there. But I repeat the documents can come in as what they are, medical documents from the treatment of I think the eye of the accused in Belgrade sometime in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do I understand then from the Prosecutor that you wouldn't be challenging the authenticity of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, I just saw them 30 seconds. They appear to be authentic to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll admit them as documents that are relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, one number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents will be added to Exhibit D340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it. You may now leave. Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have something else to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to mention the next witness, but I will wait until this witness leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may now leave, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness -- Ms. Edgerton. You're not the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I'm not, Your Honours, but in the event she's going to be brought through this door, I would just like to indicate I have a submission I'd like to make to Your Honours before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The submission is respect to the documents that are, I understand, intended to be tendered into evidence through this witness, Your Honour, and I received a list of them. There's 151 of them. I received a list on the 17th of July, two days ago, or the 19th, and I've looked at the whole list and read those documents that I'm able to, but there are 62 documents on that list, Your Honours, that aren't translated at all. And with respect to, first of all, those 62 documents, I'm having some difficulty in understanding why we might be in a position to deal with them today without translation. So I would submit that those documents shouldn't actually and aren't properly part of the Trial Record unless they're translated. It would be, in my submission, unfair and indeed wouldn't allow any of us to have a full appreciation of their potential relevance to the case. There are 14 documents on the list that are only translated in some excerpts, small portions of them, and earlier in this trial with the witness whose name was Dragas, he testified at page 7117, with that witness we saw that indeed some very significant portions were left untranslated that would help all of us, Your Honours, again, assess the document's relevance to the case. In fact, those untranslated portions in that case dealt with -- specifically with the activities of the SRK as of the date of the document. So I have difficulty with those documents coming in through this witness without translation. And as for the remaining 74, I've read all of those and would be prepared to make submissions with respect to the relevance of a large number of those. However, they're all translated. And I just want to underline with respect to those 74 that are translated, I have no issue. The Prosecution takes no issue with respect to the authenticity of the documents if this is what this witness is coming to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let me hear Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I could also venture to give an explanation. However, since my learned friend dealt with the relevance and since this -- since my colleague has dealt with the relevance and since we have discussed the matter, the two -- concerning the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't deal with relevance now, just the issue of translation. The relevance is an issue that will be taken up when the witness testifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we intended to ask for the documents to be admitted and marked for identification. The documents were submitted for translation, but the documents themselves are very short. They only contain several sentences each, and they will be fully translated by the end of the Defence case, and I believe that they will certainly be translated in August when we resume, perhaps even before. At any rate, our intention was to ask that these documents be admitted with an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, are they amenable to that treatment?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can't read them at all to even see that. I -- if there was some pearl of evidence that would affect the resolution of this case one way or another, I have no appreciation of the language to be able to answer Your Honours on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear the witness, and we'll deal first with those that are translated. Are you hearing, Mr. Tapuskovic? We'll deal first with -- what is it, 70 -- my mathematics are not so good.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Seventy-four by my count, and my mathematics are generally poorer than yours, but 74 by my count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That means you're at the very bottom of the heap, Ms. Edgerton. So we'll deal with those first that have been translated, Mr. Tapuskovic. Only those that have been translated. And when you're finished dealing with those, we'll take up the question of those that have not been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, can you tell your full name to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: [In English] My name is Snezana Marinkovic-Jekic [Interpretation] Apologies. I apologise. I started speaking in English, and I will be giving my testimony in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But please speak slower. You were born on the 13th of July, 1968; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Jesenica, Slovenia where your father worked at the time?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your primary and secondary education in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You graduated from the law school in Belgrade in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were admitted to the bar, to the bar of Serbia in Belgrade, back in 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether over these 13 years you also dealt with criminal law?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a lawyer in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you become involved in the work of the Defence team for General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: In February of 2005, in early February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that was based on whose decision?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Based on -- or, rather, pursuant to the decision of the Registry of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties within your assignment?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: I mostly dealt with the searches through documents based on the instructions provided by the counsel and co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When were you mostly dealing with documents? In what time period?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly when we were given access to the archives. That is to say the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of Republika Srpska. We were given access to the archives of the VRS, and I started examining the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Let us take it step-by-step in order to explain this fully. Can you tell the Judges what the procedure was like before you and other members of the Defence team started taking steps to examine the archives of both armies for the purposes of the Defence in this case?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: The procedure was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for my question to be entered in the transcript and then start giving your answer.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: This was the procedure: The -- the main counsel would send a request seeking access to the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This request would be sent to the Ministry of Defence of -- of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Based on their authorisation, we were allowed access to the archives, and we were allowed to examine the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Let me add this: The other archives we used was the archives of the army of Republika Srpska. The procedure this involved was such that a request seeking access to the archives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Was sent through the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not to raise any objection except to point out that there is not a single document of these 151 that emanates according to the Defence list from the archives of the Republika Srpska. So may I respectfully suggest we move on to the archives of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? And the documents on the list emanate from either the Office of the Prosecutor or, according to Defence records, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the archives of the army of Republika Srpska are not relevant, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would not wish to nit-pick this. However, there were two documents only from the archives of the VRS that we placed on this list, and they are among the other ones there you will see that later on. The documents in question are number 181 and 182 -- or 186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that explains the reference to the -- to those archives, yes. Can we now move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, in that case I apologise because they weren't indicated on my list as being from the VRS archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Marinkovic, as concerns the work you did in the archives of the VRS, whenever you wanted to gain access to the archives was it necessary to present a request for each and every occasion?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: On the occasion of every single visit to the archives we had to bring along a request in which we had to specify which part of the archives we were interested in. This request we would send to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Every authorisation they issued addressed the specific request we submitted on a given occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us roughly when it was that we filed such a request, and when was it possible to start examining the archives?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: The first request was filed in either July or August of 2006. Subsequently, we filed other requests, and we visited the archives on several occasions. The bulk of the documents contained on this list was obtained based on the authorisations we received in November and December. We, therefore, visited the archives twice, once in -- on the 1st of November -- or, rather, in November, and the second occasion was -- or -- and twice in December of 2006, and on these occasions we selected 4.000 documents, some of which are contained on the list here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Once you went through these documents, what did you do next? Did you produce a list of sorts?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Once we searched through the documents, I marked those documents which in accordance with the instructions from Defence counsel were -- I deemed significant. Next, I produced a list for my own purposes in order to be able to see whether all the documents marked as significant were in fact received later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you in fact receive all 4.000 of the documents which you produced on that list?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received all these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you receive them, if you can give us the date. And I'm referring to the documents that you selected back in December.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: The documents were received on the 30th of January, 2007, and on the 2nd of February, 2007. I personally was handed these documents at the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you have a document which certificates that you were handed each and every one of these documents from the archives of -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Out of 4.000-odd documents you are aware that a number of these documents have already been admitted into evidence in this case based on the request of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you arrived in The Hague on this occasion, did you go through the list of the documents contained in this large binder and which are contained in this list which we intend to tender into evidence pending the Trial Chamber's decision?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA MARINKOVIC-JEKIC
utterances.text: I have gone through the list, and I have gone through all the documents which have been appended to the list. And I can confirm that all the documents contained in the list are the documents which I took from the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, they are copies of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
